extracted.intended_audience: ACL/Computational Linguistics program chairs, editors, reviewers, and the wider computational linguistics research community
extracted.subtask_description: Proposed standards and procedural changes for selecting reviewers, ensuring review quality, and increasing transparency for ACL-related conferences and journals. Focuses on reviewer databases, open peer review, and reviewer training to raise overall review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for qualified reviewers / subfield expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers for specialized areas need to be ‘insiders’, well-versed in the latest developments in the sub-area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because computational linguistics is increasingly specialized (e.g., parsing, machine translation), reviewers must have up-to-date, area-specific technical knowledge; selecting non-experts leads to poor endorsement/erroneous rejections and misjudgment of papers' merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reviewer selection based on informal social networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are currently selected based on informal social networks, which limits the pool and can bias selections to those who share a particular point-of-view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on personal connections and memory of past reviewer performance is limiting and can result in inappropriate selections; improved information management is needed to expand and de-bias reviewer selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACL Reviewer Database — profile fields to record
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a public ACL database of reviewer profiles recording reviewer name and affiliation, the name and type of forum (conference, workshop, journal, etc.), its time and place, the number of papers reviewed, and the reviewer’s areas of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Program Chair or Editor (assisted by conference/journal management software) would update the database whenever reviews are produced. To protect privacy, information about which specific papers were assigned to a reviewer should not be revealed. Many conferences already publish reviewer lists, so this is an incremental step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reviewer database to classify reviewers (specialist/generalist, prolific/occasional, skill level)
rubrics_metrics.description: The database should allow a forum organizer or editor to determine, at least semi-automatically, categories of reviewers such as specialist/generalist, prolific/occasional, and skill level (e.g., journal paper vs. workshop reviewing, senior vs. extended PC experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semi-automatic categorization helps match papers to appropriately experienced reviewers and facilitates selection beyond informal networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and recognize reviewer impact (reviewer impact factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Track how many journal and conference articles a person has reviewed and how many articles were submitted to those venues; compute a reviewer’s impact factor by dividing the former by the latter, with normalization parameters (e.g., accounting for publishing activity in subfields).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantifying reviewing activity can recognize well-respected reviewers and help evaluate reviewer contributions; include normalization to account for differences across subfields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review — signing reviews to increase accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use signed reviews (visible to the author or public) to raise the stakes on review quality by making reviewers accountable for the quality of their reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different venues implement reviewer transparency differently (always require signed reviews, optional signing, or anonymous). Evidence (BMJ randomized trial) showed signing did not lower review quality or recommendations; signing has not led to increased litigation in journals using it. Signed reviews may theoretically reduce harshness, but in practice this has not been observed sufficiently to outweigh accountability benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review — publish full publication history (versions, reviews, author responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide public access to the publication history of articles: all previous versions of the paper along with their reviews and author responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication histories (as used by BMC journals and ACP) are instructive to prospective authors and reviewers and create a collective memory of reviews and prior submissions. This aids learning and helps avoid reviewers failing to recall prior versions reviewed elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require reviewer training (online course, exercises, and enforced recency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide formal reviewer training (e.g., an online course specific to the journal/conference) that every reviewer for that forum should take, with the conference/journal management software checking that the course has been completed within the last couple of years before allowing the reviewer to proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training can be self-study but treated as more stringent than merely reading guidelines. BMJ materials (PowerPoint on best practices, written exercises, practice reviews compared with editor critiques) are cited examples; randomized evidence (Schroter et al. 2004) shows trained reviewers detect significantly more major errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use practice reviews and annotated published reviews as training exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Have potential reviewers read published reviews of several articles and do practice reviews, comparing their assessments with published reviews and editor critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under open peer review or with appropriate permissions, collect published reviews and use them for hands-on exercises (e.g., reading and assessing referee reports, practice reviewing a paper and comparing with published reviews) to improve reviewers' error detection and calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach reviewing methods in classroom and seminar settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss reviewing methods in classroom settings, particularly in seminar courses where papers are read and jointly discussed, to engender improved review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to online/self-study training, integrating review practice and discussion into academic coursework helps build reviewing skills and community norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control to prevent hurried/slipshod reviews and encourage bold research
rubrics_metrics.description: Address lack of review quality caused by hurried reviewing and excessive demands on reviewers’ time, which can result in favoring safe, incremental papers instead of novel models and directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement interventions (better reviewer selection, training, open review, recognition) to improve review quality. Recognize that proliferation of conferences competes for reviewers’ time; systems should aim to reduce rushed decision-making and its conservative bias.
